questions.stem: The Khmer Empire was centred on Angkor, in what is now which country?
options: Vietnam
Indonesia
Cambodia
Thailand
questions.explanation: Angkor lies in north-western Cambodia, near the great lake Tonle Sap, whose fish and floodwaters supported a large population. At its height the empire also ruled parts of modern Thailand, Laos and Vietnam. Indonesia was home to other kingdoms, which built temples such as Borobudur on Java.

questions.stem: Which king is traditionally said to have founded the Khmer Empire in 802 CE?
options: Suryavarman II
Yasovarman I
Jayavarman II
Jayavarman VII
questions.explanation: Inscriptions record that Jayavarman II was proclaimed universal ruler (chakravartin) in a ceremony on the Kulen hills in 802, and this is taken as the founding of the empire. Yasovarman I later built a capital at Angkor itself, around 900. Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat and Jayavarman VII built Angkor Thom, both centuries later.

questions.stem: Which influences reached the Khmer from India through trade and contact?
options: Confucian exams, and Chinese characters for official writing
Hindu and Buddhist religion, and Sanskrit for inscriptions
Islam, and the Arabic script used for all royal records
Christianity, and Latin used in prayers and laws
questions.explanation: Long before Angkor, merchants and priests travelling between India and China brought Hindu and Buddhist beliefs, ideas about kingship and the Sanskrit language to mainland South-East Asia. Khmer kings used Sanskrit for many temple inscriptions, alongside Old Khmer. Islam and Christianity played no part in Angkor's religion.

questions.stem: What was the devaraja cult associated with Khmer kings?
options: An order of Buddhist monks that controlled all the temples and their rice lands
The team of engineers responsible for the city's reservoirs and canals
A royal cult that linked the king closely to a god, giving his rule divine authority
A council of nobles that met to elect each new king whenever the old king died
questions.explanation: The devaraja ('god-king') cult, begun under Jayavarman II, tied the king to a Hindu god, usually Shiva, and helped present his power as sacred; historians still debate exactly what the rituals involved. Kings were not elected by nobles, and succession was often fought over within the royal family. Kings also called themselves chakravartin, 'universal ruler'.

questions.stem: To which Hindu god was Angkor Wat originally dedicated?
options: Brahma
Indra
Vishnu
Shiva
questions.explanation: Angkor Wat was built in the first half of the 1100s by King Suryavarman II and dedicated to Vishnu, unlike most earlier Khmer state temples, which honoured Shiva. Its western orientation may be linked to Vishnu or to funeral ideas. It later became a Buddhist site and remains one today.

questions.stem: The five central towers of Angkor Wat, surrounded by walls and a wide moat, were designed to represent:
options: the Himalayan peaks that the Khmer armies had conquered
the five great kings who ruled before Suryavarman II
the volcanoes whose ash had made the Khmer rice fields fertile
Mount Meru, home of the gods at the centre of the universe
questions.explanation: Khmer temple-mountains model the universe of Hindu and Buddhist belief: the central towers are the five peaks of Mount Meru, the walls are the mountain ranges around it and the moat is the cosmic ocean. The Khmer never reached the Himalayas. The design shows how the king presented himself as ruling at the centre of the world.

questions.stem: Which achievements are linked to Jayavarman VII (ruled from 1181)?
options: Founding the empire in 802 and introducing Theravada Buddhism to it
Defending Angkor against the Thai attack of 1431 and then rebuilding its walls
Driving out the Cham invaders, building Angkor Thom and founding hospitals
Building Angkor Wat for Vishnu and moving the capital to Phnom Penh
questions.explanation: After the Cham sacked Angkor in 1177, Jayavarman VII defeated them, built the walled city of Angkor Thom with the Bayon temple at its centre, and recorded in inscriptions that he founded over 100 hospitals and many rest houses along the roads. Angkor Wat had been built earlier by Suryavarman II. Jayavarman VII followed Mahayana Buddhism, not the Theravada Buddhism that spread later.

questions.stem: Which religion did Jayavarman VII make central to his reign, building the Bayon with its many huge carved faces?
options: Shinto
Confucianism
Mahayana Buddhism
Theravada Buddhism
questions.explanation: Jayavarman VII was a Mahayana Buddhist, and the serene faces on the Bayon's towers are usually linked to the Buddhist figure Lokeshvara, perhaps combined with the king himself. Theravada Buddhism spread among the Khmer later, from the 1200s onwards. Shinto is the native religion of Japan.

questions.stem: What were the barays built around Angkor?
options: Floating markets held each week on the waters of the Tonle Sap lake
Royal roads linking Angkor to the ports of southern India
Huge rectangular reservoirs built to store and manage water
Stone towers carved with the faces of the Khmer kings
questions.explanation: The barays were enormous rectangular reservoirs; the West Baray is about 8 kilometres long and 2 kilometres wide. They were part of a network of canals, moats and dykes that managed the heavy monsoon rains. The carved faces are on the towers of the Bayon, and the Khmer roads linked Angkor to towns within the empire.

questions.stem: Archaeologists have long debated Angkor's barays and canals. What is that debate mainly about?
options: Whether they mainly irrigated rice fields or mainly had religious and symbolic purposes
Whether they were built by the Khmer or added later by French colonial engineers
Whether they held salt water piped inland from the sea or fresh water from the rivers
Whether they were dug before the last ice age or much later, in the reign of Jayavarman II
questions.explanation: The 'hydraulic city' theory argued that the reservoirs irrigated rice fields to feed a huge population, while critics argued they were mainly symbolic, representing the oceans around Mount Meru. Recent LiDAR surveys and excavations show a vast, complex water network, and many researchers now think it served practical and religious purposes. The barays were certainly Khmer works.

options: A Chinese envoy who visited Angkor in 1296–1297 and wrote about daily life
A French explorer who made Angkor famous in Europe during the 1860s
A Khmer king who built the walled city of Angkor Thom and the Bayon
A Thai general whose army captured Angkor and carried off its statues and treasures
questions.explanation: Zhou Daguan travelled with a Chinese diplomatic mission and later wrote The Customs of Cambodia, the only detailed eyewitness account of Angkor to survive from its time. He described the king's processions, houses, markets, festivals and farming. The French explorer who publicised Angkor in Europe was Henri Mouhot.

questions.stem: What did Zhou Daguan notice about trade in the markets of Angkor?
options: Trade was banned, and the king shared out all goods
Most of the trading was done by women
Only Chinese merchants were allowed to trade
All goods were paid for with gold coins made by the king
questions.explanation: Zhou Daguan wrote that it was women who knew how to trade, so Chinese merchants who settled there often married local women partly for their business skills. The Khmer did not mint coins; people traded with rice, cloth, gold and silver by weight and Chinese goods. His account is a key source for the role of women at Angkor.

questions.stem: Why are the carved bas-reliefs of the Bayon valuable evidence for historians?
options: They are diaries carved by ordinary farmers that list their crops, animals and family members
They were carved by French artists in the 1800s to show how Angkor might have looked
They record the exact population of Angkor and the taxes each family paid
As well as battles with the Cham, they show daily life such as fishing, cooking and markets
questions.explanation: Alongside scenes of war elephants and naval battles with the Cham on the Tonle Sap, the Bayon reliefs show ordinary people fishing, cooking, trading, playing games and giving birth, so they reveal everyday life that inscriptions ignore. They are carvings from Jayavarman VII's time, not written records. Combined with Zhou Daguan's account, they give a picture of life beyond the palace.

questions.stem: In 1431, according to the traditional account, Angkor was attacked by forces from which kingdom?
options: Champa
The Mongol Yuan Empire
Majapahit
Ayutthaya
questions.explanation: Ayutthaya, a Thai kingdom to the west, attacked Angkor several times, and the sack traditionally dated to 1431 is often given as the end of the Angkor period, as the Khmer court later moved south towards Phnom Penh. The Cham, from Champa, had sacked Angkor much earlier, in 1177. The Mongol Yuan dynasty sent the embassy that Zhou Daguan travelled with, but never conquered Angkor.

questions.stem: Tree-ring records from the region show long droughts broken by extremely heavy monsoons during the 1300s and 1400s. How does this evidence add to explanations of the decline of Angkor?
options: It proves the reservoirs were never used, because there was never enough rain to fill them
It suggests climate swings damaged the water system, adding to pressures such as Thai attacks
It proves that the Thai attacks never happened and that climate was the only cause of decline
It shows that Angkor was abandoned in a single year after one flood destroyed the whole city
questions.explanation: Researchers argue that decades of drought followed by intense floods damaged Angkor's canals and reservoirs, making it harder to feed the city. Most historians see this as one factor alongside attacks from Ayutthaya, the shift of trade towards the coast and the spread of Theravada Buddhism. Angkor declined over a long period and was never completely abandoned; Angkor Wat stayed an active Buddhist site.

questions.stem: One theory links the decline of Angkor as a royal centre to the spread of Theravada Buddhism from the 1200s. What is the reasoning behind it?
options: It banned rice farming, so the people of Angkor could no longer grow enough food
It forbade building in stone, so no new temples, bridges or reservoirs could be built at all
It required all believers to move to Sri Lanka, emptying the city of its workers
Its focus on monks and personal merit weakened the god-king idea behind huge state temples
questions.explanation: Theravada Buddhism centred on monasteries, monks and each person earning merit, so it gave less support to the idea of a god-king commanding vast labour to build stone temple-mountains. Large temple building at Angkor largely stopped after Jayavarman VII. This is one theory among several, and it works alongside climate, war and trade explanations rather than replacing them.
